claims.text: Rapid high-temperature synthesis can form and disperse sub-100 nm high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles on defective carbon supports.
Defective turbostratic graphite contains numerous edge-plane sites that can anchor metallic nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles can partially intercalate and take root at edge planes of defective turbostratic graphite.
Interaction with defective turbostratic graphite produces strong nanoparticle anchoring and high binding energy.
Defect-site anchoring reduces the mobility of surface atoms in HEA nanoparticles.
Surface-atom diffusion causes nanoparticle coalescence and premelting.
Suppressing surface-atom diffusion delays the onset of premelting.
Defective-carbon anchoring raises the effective premelting temperature of HEA nanoparticles.
Carbon-support anchoring can provide excellent thermal stability to nanoparticles during high-temperature processing.
HEA nanoparticles on defective carbon will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than otherwise identical nanoparticles on inert or highly graphitized low-defect carbon.
HEA nanoparticles on defective carbon will have a higher melting temperature than the low-defect-support baseline.
HEA nanoparticles on defective carbon will exhibit a sharper melting transition than the low-defect-support baseline.
A sharper melting transition indicates enhanced nanoparticle thermal stability.
The proposed anchoring effect should apply to HEA nanoparticles below approximately 100 nm.
The effect may disappear when the carbon-support defect density is too low.
Support anchoring becomes less dominant for nanoparticles significantly larger than 100 nm.
The defective- and low-defect-support samples should be prepared to differ only in support defect density and then heated under identical conditions.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in premelting or melting temperature on the defective support would falsify the proposed anchoring mechanism.
